title: NURS 1017 Unit 5 Case Study 3
description: 28-year-old female presenting with photosensitive malar butterfly erythema and arthralgias (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus), evaluated alongside clinical differentiation of plaque psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, and cutaneous drug eruptions.

question.stem: The nurse conducts an intake examination for Maya. Which assessment cues should the nurse recognize as hallmark manifestations of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and inflammatory cutaneous pathology? Select all that apply.

options.text: Marked photosensitivity with acute flare of facial erythema, burning, and malaise following 30 minutes of direct sunlight exposure
Painless, superficial ulcerations on the hard palate and buccal mucosa
Well-demarcated thick plaques covered with coarse silvery-white scales located strictly over the extensor surfaces of both elbows
Fixed, erythematous, flat to slightly raised 'butterfly-shaped' rash spanning symmetrically across the bilateral cheeks and nasal bridge while sparing the nasolabial folds
Intensely pruritic lichenified plaques in the bilateral antecubital and popliteal flexural creases with personal history of asthma
Bilateral symmetric swelling, warmth, and stiffness of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) hand joints

question.explanation: Maya presents with classic diagnostic criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE): (Option 4) Characteristic malar 'butterfly' rash (erythema over the malar eminences and bridge of the nose, classically sparing the nasolabial folds); (Option 1) Photosensitivity (cutaneous rash triggered or worsened by ultraviolet sunlight); (Option 6) Non-erosive polyarthritis affecting small joints (MCP, PIP); and (Option 2) Oral/nasopharyngeal mucosal ulcers. Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces (elbows/knees) characterize plaque psoriasis. Lichenified pruritic plaques in flexural folds (antecubital, popliteal) with an asthma history characterize atopic dermatitis.

question.stem: The nurse analyzes the pathophysiology of chronic inflammatory and allergic dermatoses. For each clinical condition, click to specify its primary immunopathological mechanism and characteristic anatomical distribution.

rows.text: Type III hypersensitivity autoimmune disorder with immune-complex deposition producing photosensitive butterfly malar erythema sparing nasolabial folds
T-cell driven autoimmune inflammatory disorder causing rapid epidermal hyperproliferation and silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces (elbows/knees)
Chronic relapsing pruritic disorder associated with the atopic triad, characterized by dry, cracked, lichenified plaques in flexural skin creases
Type IV cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction resulting from topical sensitization to antigens like nickel or poison ivy, mimicking the shape of contact
Psoriatic arthritis of small joints, pinpoint bleeding upon scale removal (Auspitz sign), and punctate nail pitting or onycholysis

question.preamble: Laboratory serology, antinuclear antibodies, and inflammatory markers have been reported. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1100 and the Laboratory & Serology Reports.
question.explanation:
1. Lupus Erythematosus (SLE): Type III immune-complex hypersensitivity where circulating autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith) form complexes that deposit in dermoepidermal junctions, blood vessels, and kidneys, creating photosensitive malar rashes and multisystem inflammation.
2. Psoriasis: T-lymphocyte driven autoimmune dermatosis where inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-17, IL-23) accelerate keratinocyte cell turnover from ~28 days down to 3–4 days, producing thickened erythematous plaques capped with micaceous silvery scales classically on extensor surfaces, accompanied by nail pitting and psoriatic arthritis in ~30%.
3. Atopic Dermatitis: Pruritic chronic inflammatory eczema linked to epidermal barrier gene defects (filaggrin) and IgE dysregulation, manifesting as flexural lichenification.
4. Allergic Contact Dermatitis: Type IV delayed-type cell-mediated hypersensitivity triggered by sensitized T-cells reacting to haptens (poison ivy urushiol, nickel jewelry, neomycin), forming pruritic vesicular eruptions mirroring the contact area.

question.stem:
The nurse synthesizes Maya's clinical cues and laboratory markers to prioritize systemic risks.

Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1300.
question.explanation:
1. Type III Hypersensitivity: In SLE, autoantibodies against nuclear antigens (ANA, anti-dsDNA) form antigen-antibody complexes. These circulating immune complexes deposit in capillary basement membranes of skin, glomeruli, joints, and serosa, activating complement (consuming C3/C4) and recruiting neutrophils that cause tissue injury.
2. Photosensitivity: UV radiation damages keratinocytes, prompting apoptosis and cellular blebbing that displays nuclear debris at the cell surface. This provides a surge of autoantigens that binds autoantibodies, triggering severe cutaneous inflammation (malar flare) and systemic disease exacerbations.
3. Renal Priority: Lupus nephritis occurs in up to 50% of SLE patients and is a leading cause of morbidity/mortality. Proteinuria and hematuria signal glomerular immune complex deposition, requiring immediate nephrology surveillance.

question.stem: The nurse formulates the comprehensive education and self-management plan for Maya. Which nursing interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Instruct Maya to monitor for signs of renal flare, including sudden weight gain, peripheral leg swelling, or foamy/frothy urine, and report them promptly
Instruct Maya to apply broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF ≥ 50) daily, wear sun-protective clothing, and avoid direct midday sunlight to prevent disease flares
Educate Maya on the importance of baseline and annual ophthalmological examinations while taking hydroxychloroquine to screen for retinal toxicity
Encourage Maya to use commercial sunlamps and tanning beds during winter months to keep her skin warm and improve joint stiffness
Advise balancing rest with low-impact physical exercise to reduce joint stiffness and combat chronic fatigue without overexertion
Instruct Maya to abruptly discontinue prescribed oral corticosteroids as soon as her facial rash fades

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1430.
question.explanation: Appropriate nursing education for SLE includes: (Option 2) Rigorous photoprotection (SPF 50+, protective clothing, avoiding sun) because UV light directly triggers cutaneous and systemic flares; (Option 3) Annual dilated ophthalmology exams for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy (maculopathy/bull's-eye damage); (Option 1) Surveillance for renal impairment (foamy urine indicating proteinuria, edema, hypertension); and (Option 5) Energy conservation and pacing for lupus fatigue. Tanning beds emit intense UV radiation that can provoke catastrophic lupus flares. Corticosteroids must never be stopped abruptly due to the risk of life-threatening secondary adrenal crisis.

question.stem: The nurse reviews clinical actions and medication safety for inflammatory skin disorders, including drug-induced cutaneous eruptions. For each action, click to specify whether the intervention is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Assess the client for new-onset widespread morbilliform rash, facial swelling, or mucosal bullae following initiation of any new systemic pharmaceutical agent
Instruct a client with psoriasis to aggressively scratch and peel off thick silvery plaques down to bleeding dermis to accelerate skin shedding
Advise a client with suspected allergic contact dermatitis to undergo patch testing to identify specific sensitized allergens (e.g., nickel, fragrances)
Encourage a client with active atopic dermatitis to take long, hot bubble baths with perfumed bath salts twice daily
Monitor blood pressure and obtain routine urinalysis at every outpatient rheumatology visit to track renal vascular health in SLE
Perform continuous invasive arterial line blood pressure monitoring during routine outpatient clinic appointments

question.preamble: The nurse is evaluating comparative dermatological safety and client education. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1530.
question.explanation:
1. Indicated: Cutaneous drug eruptions range from mild symmetric morbilliform exanthems to fatal Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) with epidermal detachment; vigilance with new medications is critical.
2. Contraindicated: In psoriasis, forcibly removing scales triggers the Koebner phenomenon (new psoriatic lesions induced by local trauma) and Auspitz sign (punctate bleeding).
3. Indicated: Patch testing is the gold standard diagnostic tool for confirming Type IV cell-mediated allergic contact dermatitis.
4. Contraindicated: Hot water, long baths, and fragranced bubble baths strip lipids from the skin barrier, exacerbating xerosis and triggering intense pruritus in atopic dermatitis.
5. Indicated: Regular BP and urinalysis detect asymptomatic early lupus nephritis and renal vasculopathy.
6. Non-Essential: Invasive arterial monitoring is inappropriate for outpatient clinics.
